title: Solving efficiency problems
prior_knowledge_summary: From Lesson 7, efficiency is useful output divided by matching total input.
From Lesson 7, efficiency may be written as a decimal or percentage, and useful plus non-useful energy equals total input.
From Lesson 7, energy ratios and power ratios are both valid when numerator and denominator describe the same system operation.
new_learning: Select matching energy quantities or matching power quantities for an efficiency calculation.
Rearrange the efficiency relationship to find an unknown input or useful output.
Compare systems fairly when useful output size and efficiency lead to different rankings.
not_yet_taught: Define power as work done per unit time or use P = W/t.
Use gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy or electrical circuit formulas unless all required energy or power values are supplied.
Analyse thermal processes or wave intensity as a required part of an efficiency calculation.

blocks.heading: Where did the rest go?
content: A lifting machine receives 500 J but raises a load by only 350 J. It has not destroyed 150 J. Energy has spread to non-useful stores, perhaps as heating or sound.
The useful question is not just how much energy arrived. It is what fraction of the total input became the intended output.

figure.purpose: Create the need to compare useful output with total input.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a machine receiving a 500 J arrow, sending a 350 J useful lifting arrow and a 150 J heating-and-sound arrow. Keep the output branches visually distinct without showing an efficiency result.
figure.alt_text: A machine divides 500 joules of input into 350 joules of useful lifting and 150 joules transferred to other stores.

blocks.heading: The relationship to remember
content: The formula to remember is $\eta = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$.
Here $\eta$ is efficiency. It has no unit because the numerator and denominator have the same unit. Use energy over energy, both in joules, or power over power, both in watts.
For a percentage, multiply the decimal efficiency by 100. A decimal efficiency of 0.70 is the same as 70%.

controlled_formula.latex: \eta = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}

figure.purpose: Separate the two valid matching forms of the efficiency ratio.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison with one energy-over-energy fraction in joules and one power-over-power fraction in watts. Cross out energy-over-power and label it mismatched units. Do not include practice values.
figure.alt_text: Efficiency uses energy divided by energy or power divided by power, never a mixture of the two.

blocks.heading: Start by naming the two sides
content: A conveyor receives 8.0 kJ and transfers 5.6 kJ usefully to packages. First label the useful output as 5.6 kJ and the total input as 8.0 kJ.
Check the physics: useful output is smaller than total input, so the efficiency must be below 1, or below 100%. The kilojoules cancel because both quantities use the same unit.

figure.purpose: Model a complete direct efficiency calculation and limit check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout: circle total input 8.0 kJ, underline useful output 5.6 kJ, place them in the correct ratio, convert 0.70 to 70 percent, then show a final less-than-100-percent check.
figure.alt_text: Dividing 5.6 kilojoules of useful output by 8.0 kilojoules of input gives an efficiency of 70 percent.

blocks.heading: Rearrange before substituting
content: If useful output and efficiency are known, the total input must be larger. Rearrange to $E_{\text{in}} = E_{\text{useful}}/\eta$ or $P_{\text{in}} = P_{\text{useful}}/\eta$.
If total input and efficiency are known, multiply: $E_{\text{useful}} = \eta E_{\text{in}}$ or $P_{\text{useful}} = \eta P_{\text{in}}$.
Example: a 65% efficient motor delivers 780 W usefully. Convert 65% to 0.65, then $P_{\text{in}}=780/0.65=1200$ W. Dividing by a number below 1 correctly makes the input larger.

figure.purpose: Teach the direction of the two rearrangements.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-path flow. Path one: input times efficiency gives useful output. Path two: useful output divided by efficiency gives input. Include 780 W and 0.65 only on the second path and end at 1200 W.
figure.alt_text: Multiply input by efficiency to find useful output, or divide useful output by efficiency to find input.

blocks.heading: A reverse problem still uses one ratio
content: A hoist transfers 1.62 kJ usefully and is 67.5% efficient. The unknown is the total input, so first write $0.675=1.62/E_{\text{in}}$.
$E_{\text{in}}=1.62/0.675=2.40$ kJ. Carry the unit and the unrounded value into the energy check.
The non-useful transfer is $2.40-1.62=0.780$ kJ, and $1.62+0.780=2.40$ kJ recovers the input.
The input is larger than the useful output. This direction check catches the common mistake of multiplying by efficiency when the input is unknown.

figure.purpose: Show a safe reverse-efficiency method with an independent energy check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked flow. Start with useful output 1.62 kJ and efficiency 67.5 percent, convert to 0.675, divide to obtain 2.40 kJ input, then show 1.62 plus 0.780 equals 2.40 kJ. Highlight that input must be larger than useful output.
figure.alt_text: Useful output divided by decimal efficiency gives total input, which is checked by adding useful and non-useful transfers.

blocks.heading: Why a large output does not guarantee high efficiency
content: It feels reasonable to call the machine with the larger useful output more efficient. That can fail because efficiency is a ratio, not an output amount.
Machine A gives 900 W from 1200 W, so its efficiency is 75%. Machine B gives 1000 W from 1600 W, so its efficiency is 62.5%. Machine B gives more useful power but is less efficient.
Always compare each useful output with its own total input. Also reject efficiencies above 1 or 100% for an ordinary energy-conversion system.

figure.purpose: Contrast output size with the output-to-input ratio.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper side-by-side machines. Machine A has 1200 W in and 900 W useful out. Machine B has 1600 W in and 1000 W useful out. Show efficiency bars of 75 percent and 62.5 percent to expose why larger output alone is not enough.
figure.alt_text: A machine with larger useful output can still be less efficient if its total input is much larger.

blocks.heading: Compare ratios, not output sizes
content: First identify the intended useful output and the total input. Second choose energy over energy or power over power. Third convert a percentage to a decimal before rearranging.
Calculate without early rounding, then give a sensible final precision. Check that input is at least as large as useful output and that efficiency lies from 0 to 1, or from 0% to 100%.
When comparing two machines, calculate each useful-output-to-input ratio. A machine can deliver more useful power yet be less efficient because its total input is also much larger.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact decision and checking routine for unfamiliar contexts.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper decision map: label useful and input, match quantity type, convert percent, rearrange, calculate, then check zero to one. End with two side-by-side machines and the instruction compare ratios, not output sizes.
figure.alt_text: A decision map calculates efficiency and compares machine ratios rather than useful output sizes alone.

concepts_taught: efficiency as a matching output-to-input ratio
fair comparison of systems with different input and useful output
misconceptions_addressed: The largest useful output must be the most efficient.
Energy may be divided directly by power.
A percentage may be substituted without converting it to a decimal.
Useful output may exceed total input.
next_lesson_can_assume: Select matching energy or power quantities for efficiency.
Find efficiency, input or useful output.
Convert between decimal and percentage efficiency.
Compare systems using their efficiency ratios and check physical limits.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Define power as work done per unit time or use P = W/t.
Calculate gravitational potential or kinetic energy without supplied formulas.
Analyse circuit power without supplied relationships.
